headline: Leef Brands says rescheduling cut its Q3 tax bill by 95%
dek: California extractor Leef Brands stopped applying Section 280E to medical sales, and its Q3 2026 tax expense fell to $56,013 from $1.04 million a year earlier.
key_points: Leef Brands booked $56,013 of income tax expense in Q3 2026, down from $1,038,063 a year earlier, a drop of about 95%.
The company told the SEC it no longer applies Section 280E to qualifying medical cannabis sales from 1 July 2026, and possibly from 1 January.
Its uncertain tax liabilities still rose to $22.8 million from $15.2 million, because adult-use sales remain under 280E.
Leef is the latest company to pick its own start date for relief while the IRS and Treasury have not issued full guidance.
body: Leef Brands, a small California cannabis extraction company, has put a hard number on what the April rescheduling order is worth to a medical seller. In its third-quarter report filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on 16 November, the company recorded $56,013 of income tax expense for the three months to 30 September, against $1,038,063 in the same quarter of 2025. That is a fall of about $982,000, or roughly 95%.

The filing gives one main reason: Leef now accrues Section 280E only on its adult-use sales. Section 280E bars businesses that traffic in Schedule I or II drugs from deducting ordinary costs such as rent and wages. Since the Justice Department's 23 April order moved state-licensed medical marijuana into Schedule III, Leef says the rule no longer reaches the medical side of its business.

Leef holds medical cannabis licences and says it separates medical from adult-use transactions at the point of sale. On that basis it has concluded that 280E stopped applying to qualifying medical sales from 1 July 2026, and possibly from 1 January 2026. It now books an uncertain tax position only for adult-use activity.

The company says it believes this position is more likely than not to survive an audit. It also concedes that the Internal Revenue Service could challenge it, either on whether specific sales count as medical or on how shared costs are split between the medical and adult-use books. That second point matters for any operator running both kinds of sales out of one building with one payroll.

Leef's revenue was flat to slightly lower. Net revenue was $8.07 million in the quarter, against $8.38 million a year earlier. Gross profit was $3.08 million, a 38% margin, almost unchanged. Operating expenses rose to $4.59 million from $3.27 million, mostly on wages, and the company posted an operating loss of $1.51 million.

The bottom line still turned positive. According to The Marijuana Herald's reading of the filing, Leef recorded about $282,000 of net income, compared with a $3.8 million loss a year earlier. The 10-Q shows most of that swing came from a $2.07 million gain on the fair value of a derivative liability, a non-cash item. The tax cut was the second-largest contributor.

For the first nine months of 2026, income tax expense was $1.73 million, down from $2.37 million. Yet total uncertain tax liabilities grew to $22.8 million at 30 September from $15.2 million at the end of 2025, which the company tied to continuing accruals and to liabilities taken on in an acquisition. The filing also repeats a going-concern warning, alongside an accumulated deficit of $141.5 million and a working-capital surplus of $10.8 million.
> Rescheduling relief is real, but each company is writing its own start date until the IRS writes one for everybody.

Leef's choice adds to a patchwork. As we reported on 15 November, third-quarter filings from five large multi-state operators showed $1.96 billion of uncertain tax balances and three different start dates for relief. The Marijuana Herald notes that Trulieve has recognised medical relief for all of 2026, while Curaleaf starts from 28 April and Vireo Growth from 23 April. Leef has chosen 1 July as its firm date, with 1 January as a possibility.

Our own comparison: a company that books relief from 1 January effectively claims almost four extra months of deductions compared with one that starts on 28 April. For a company the size of Leef, whose quarterly tax swing was about $982,000, that gap is material. Until Treasury and the IRS publish guidance on mixed medical and adult-use businesses, auditors and tax authorities can still second-guess every one of these choices.

Most coverage of 280E relief has focused on the big multi-state operators. Leef shows the effect on a company with about $8 million of quarterly revenue, where a $1 million annual tax swing can be the difference between a loss and a profit. Operators with medical licences that keep clean point-of-sale records of medical transactions are best placed to make the same argument. Those that cannot prove which sale was which will find it harder.

The broader rescheduling of all marijuana is still pending. The Marijuana Herald reports that final written arguments in the Drug Enforcement Administration's hearing were filed on 5 November, leaving Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius to prepare a recommendation before Administrator Terry Cole decides. A Government Accountability Office spokesperson told the outlet on 17 November that the GAO has no ongoing work on drug scheduling, though it is studying the economic effects of federal drug policies. The GAO's 23 September report, which opponents of rescheduling have cited in the hearing, found that the DEA's final decisions matched HHS recommendations for all 84 substances it finalised from 2020 through 2025, but that neither the DEA nor the FDA has full written procedures for scheduling reviews.

Watch for IRS or Treasury guidance on how mixed businesses should split costs between medical and adult-use sales; it would settle which start dates hold. Watch Judge Julius's recommendation in the DEA hearing, since adult-use rescheduling would end 280E for Leef's remaining sales. And watch Leef's annual report, which will show whether its auditors accept the 1 January date or only 1 July.
